featured.content: Genesis 13 So Abram left Egypt and traveled north into the Negev, along with his wife and Lot and all that they owned. 2 (Abram was very rich in livestock, silver, and gold.) 3 From the Negev, they continued traveling by stages toward Bethel, and they pitched their tents between Bethel and Ai, where they had camped before. 4 This was the same place where Abram had built the altar, and there he worshiped the Lord again. 5 Lot, who was traveling with Abram, had also become very wealthy with flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle, and many tents. 6 But the land could not support both Abram and Lot with all their flocks and herds living so close together. 7 So disputes broke out between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot. (At that time Canaanites and Perizzites were also living in the land.) 8 Finally Abram said to Lot, “Let’s not allow this conflict to come between us or our herdsmen. After all, we are close relatives! 9 The whole countryside is open to you. Take your choice of any section of the land you want, and we will separate. If you want the land to the left, then I’ll take the land on the right. If you prefer the land on the right, then I’ll go to the left.” 10 Lot took a long look at the fertile plains of the Jordan Valley in the direction of Zoar. The whole area was well watered everywhere, like the garden of the Lord or the beautiful land of Egypt. (This was before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) 11 Lot chose for himself the whole Jordan Valley to the east of them. He went there with his flocks and servants and parted company with his uncle Abram. 12 So Abram settled in the land of Canaan, and Lot moved his tents to a place near Sodom and settled among the cities of the plain. 13 But the people of this area were extremely wicked and constantly sinned against the Lord. 14 After Lot had gone, the Lord said to Abram, “Look as far as you can see in every direction—north and south, east and west. 15 I am giving all this land, as far as you can see, to you and your descendants[a] as a permanent possession. 16 And I will give you so many descendants that, like the dust of the earth, they cannot be counted! 17 Go and walk through the land in every direction, for I am giving it to you.” 18 So Abram moved his camp to Hebron and settled near the oak grove belonging to Mamre. There he built another altar to the Lord. At this point in the story, God’s promise to Abraham of the promised land hasn’t come true yet, but good land is part of the promise We’ve seen Abraham have faithful triumphs and failures, but this is a time when Abraham showed great faith once again because there are SEVERAL reasons why Abraham could have taken the better land 1. movement towards God’s promise of good land anyway 2. and this is probably a more striking one to me, but culturally speaking, the older would NEVER defer to the younger. Lot, as the younger, should have deferred to Abraham the older – both in going to him to resolve the disagreement between their herdsmen and in giving him the better pick of land But Abraham wasn’t fixated on culture and on manipulating God’s promises Abraham’s dealings are not in seniority, but in brotherly love and that’s what faith does. Faith resolves tension with generous self-sacrifice Christians often say in tense situations, “Well, I’m not a doormat! I deserve not to be walked all over!” But my pastor said something very striking to me. “Aren’t we glad Christ never said that?” A faithful and generous person doesn’t need to manipulate or control the situation because they are resting in the promises and sovereignty of God Faith leads to trust leads to generosity and self-sacrifice with others.

7,于是阿布拉姆和洛特的牧民之间爆发了争执. (当时,迦南人和佩里兹人也居住在该地. ) 8 最后,Abram对Lot说: " 让我们不要让这场冲突发生在我们和牧民之间。 我们毕竟是近亲! 第9条 整个农村都对你开放. 你选择你想要的土地的任何部分 我们就会分开
如果你想让土地在左边,那我就让土地在右边。 如果你喜欢右边的土地,那么我就往左边去。 10 洛特对约旦河谷向左尔方向的肥沃平原进行了长时间的考察. 整个地区到处都有良好的取水,如主的花园或埃及美丽的地.
(这是在主毁灭了索多玛和戈莫拉之前) 11 洛特自己选择了他们以东的整个约旦河谷. 他带着他的羊群和仆人去那儿,和他叔叔Abram分道扬镳。 12日,阿布拉姆在迦南地定居,洛特将帐篷搬到了索多姆附近的一个地方,并定居于平地的城市中.
13,但此地之人,极恶而常犯主. 14 在洛特离开后,主对Abram说: " 请你看看每一个方向,即北和南、东和西。 15,我把所有的土地,就你所看到的,作为永久财产,交给你和你的子孙。
十六,我给你这么多的后人,像地上的尘土一样,他们不能被统计! 17 出行,走遍地上,各行各业,我把它赏赐你们。” 18日,阿布拉姆将营地迁至希伯伦并定居在属于马姆雷的橡树林附近. 在那里他又为主建造了一座祭坛.
在故事的这一刻,上帝对亚伯拉罕的允诺还没有实现,但好地是我们所见到的亚伯拉罕有忠实的胜利和失败的诺言的一部分,但此时亚伯拉罕再次表现出了极大的信心,因为有SEVERAL的理由,亚伯拉罕可以夺取更好的地一. 走向上帝对好土地的承诺,反正是2
这对我来说可能更引人注目 但从文化上讲 年长者绝不会屈从于年轻人
作为年轻人,洛特应该把年长者留给亚伯拉罕 — — 既去他解决牧民之间的分歧,又让他选择更好的土地 — — 但亚伯拉罕并不热衷于文化和操纵上帝对亚伯拉罕的诺言 — — 亚伯拉罕的交往不是在资历上,而是在兄弟般的爱心上,而这正是信仰的作用。
信仰用慷慨自救的基督徒解决了紧张局势, 我不应该到处走! 但我的牧师对我说了一些非常引人注目的话。
“难道我们不庆幸基督从未这么说吗?” 一个忠诚而慷慨的人不需要操控或控制局势,因为他们沉浸在上帝信仰的承诺中,而主权导致信任导致与他人的慷慨和自我牺牲。

featured.content: https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/23102213/effective-evangelism.mp3 In the summer of 2021, pastor Luke Peterson moved to Columbus, Ohio, to look for lost people. To find them, he joined a gym. He started building friendships. And then he began asking those friends if they wanted to come over. “Word started getting around—‘You’re not going to believe this, but Luke’s a pastor,’” he said. ‘It created some intrigue, and people started coming. I used to have a note in my phone of how many people came to our church because I went to CrossFit Grandview. It was up to like 60 or 70 before I stopped counting because it was impossible.” Peterson’s good at evangelism, and his church is too—last year, they welcomed around 500 first-time visitors. When he preaches, he knows about half his audience is probably unchurched. Pastor Luke Peterson (right) chats with Capital Church attendees / Courtesy of Capital Church Facebook This is unusual in a country where 40 million adults have stopped attending church over the last 30 years, and where 76 percent of pastors said “fostering connections with unchurched people” is a need in their church. Much has changed since the Billy Graham rallies of the ’60s, the door-knocking of the ’80s, and seeker-sensitive church billboards of the ’90s. In the past, “you could randomly walk up to the person pumping gas next to you and say, ‘Do you know Jesus?’” said Perimeter Church pastor Jeff Norris. “Could that still work? Sure. But more and more, we tell people to invite neighbors into their home. The reality is that evangelism is much slower, and more relational, than it used to be.” Today, people aren’t as likely to read the Bible, think it’s the Word of God, or go to church . But they’re also less hostile to Christianity than they were five years ago. And while they read the Bible less—especially in Gen Z—the trajectory is moving up . “We’re not past ‘my truth, your truth,’” said Rob Warren, pastor of Doxa Church in Madison, Wisconsin. “But people aren’t as sure that their truth is actually true.” These days, evangelistically effective churches are keeping evangelism front of mind in the way they preach, train, and encourage their congregations. They’re celebrating small wins. And they’re leading with a high view of Scripture, prayer, and God’s sovereignty. “We’ve seen all of our ministries grow—from kids to youth to college ministry to Doxa Church as a whole,” Warren said. “It’s not just one demographic of people who are getting saved. God’s doing something.” Times Have Changed Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer said . Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of 20 church members to reach one person for Christ per year. Today, it takes 50, Rainer said . “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.” That trend is likely to continue. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. “I’ve got a new couple that moved into my neighborhood a while ago, and I haven’t even seen them yet,” said Daniel Simmons, executive pastor of campuses and central discipleship at The Summit Church. This means equipping the congregation is more challenging—and important—than ever before. “Evangelism can be this thing that is so burdensome and guilt-driven,” said pastor Christian Gracia. He planted King’s City Church in Las Vegas in 2024 with around 80 people and has seen the church grow to more than 400. “People can feel like they’re not ready or not good enough at evangelism,” Gracia said. “They don’t always know what to say, and can feel like a terrible Christian because they don’t do it. And I always want to help them understand that’s not true.” Start with Leadership If church leaders want to create a culture of evangelism in their church, there’s only one place to start, said Warren, who has baptized 150 people in the last eight months. “Tell me 10 people that you’ve shared the gospel with over the last month or two,” he said. “Because if the leadership team is not doing that, then it’s just an aspirational thing and you’re not going to be able to sustain it. You need those ‘just the other day’ stories.” At Perimeter, they’re putting structure around this. This PCA megachurch in Atlanta was planted by a gifted evangelist, Randy Pope, in 1977. Over the years, they’ve seen thousands come to Christ. But last spring, during a staff training, Norris noticed the focus had slipped. “What we tend to do, if left unto ourselves, if church leaders aren’t constantly pushing, is default to what is comfortable,” he said. “Church becomes more about me and my comfort or what my children need. . . . If you don’t constantly keep pushing on evangelism, it’s going to become too big of a burden and people will stop doing it.” Perimeter Church has grown largely through evangelism / Courtesy of Perimeter Church He saw this during Perimeter’s two-day staff workshop: “It became a bit more evident that most of us aren’t making disciples,” he said. “I told them—starting with the executive leadership team all the way down—that their supervisor is going to begin asking them what’s going on in their personal ministry.” This isn’t quota-driven, like “How many times have you shared the gospel this week?” It’s more along the lines of “Who are you praying for who doesn’t know Jesus?” “How are you trusting the Lord to provide opportunities for you to share the gospel with that person?” And then, “Have you been able to have those conversations? If so, how have those gone? Is there anything I can be praying for?” Over at The Summit Church, pastored by evangelist J. D. Greear, similar conversations are taking place. “We only grew 2 percent this year—we have not grown much over the past few years,” Simmons said. “We did some real soul searching in the spring, and found that our people have lost that invitation culture.” So Summit staff are reminding themselves of their goals. “Every ministry needs to know how they contribute to reaching lost people with the gospel, including the ones that may not intuitively do it,” Simmons said. “We’ve got a strong prayer ministry here. How does prayer contribute to reaching lost people? They should know that. Our deacon ministry should know how they contribute to reaching lost people. Our small group ministry should know how they contribute to reaching lost people.” Preaching As leaders begin to share their faith, it’ll come out in their conversations: “Just the other day, I was talking to a guy . . .” This is especially powerful if it comes from the pulpit—and that’s only the beginning of how pastors can use their platform to encourage the spread of the gospel. In a recent sermon, Gracia talked about truth and morality, explaining ideas such as postmodernism and cultural relativism. Christian Gracia preaching at King’s City Church in Las Vegas in October 2026 / Courtesy of King’s City Church YouTube “We’re not trying to win arguments,” he told his congregation. “I’m not trying to give you ammo for the water cooler. I’m trying to help you understand the world you live in. I’m giving you names for the water you’re swimming in, and then trying to help you navigate it. There are actually great reasons for what you believe. And there are also people who are seeking better answers than they have.” The Sunday teaching is primarily for believers. featured.title_zh: 我们需要了解我们的改革根源
featured.content: What does it mean to be Reformed? The label is used frequently but not always carefully. For some, it simply refers to a particular view of salvation. For others, it evokes a tradition, a culture, or even an aesthetic. Yet historically, to be Reformed has meant something much richer. While no single sentence can capture the fullness of the Reformed tradition, at minimum it means three things: to be biblical, to be covenantal, and to be confessional. The authority of Scripture governs our theology, covenant theology provides Scripture’s redemptive framework, and the historic confessions summarize and safeguard the church’s doctrinal convictions. Remove any one of those pillars, and something essential to the Reformed tradition is lost. With “Reformed” in its name, it’s hardly surprising that Reformed Theological Seminary has long sought to equip pastors and church members in all three areas. In recent years, members of its faculty have produced substantial volumes on the Old and New Testaments and on covenant theology. Now, with The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application , they turn their attention to the confessional foundation of the Reformed tradition. The result is a volume that seeks not only to explain what the confession teaches but also to demonstrate why confessional theology remains vital for the church today. What Is the Westminster Confession of Faith? The Westminster Confession of Faith takes its name from the Westminster Assembly, a gathering of more than 100 ministers and theologians convened by the English Parliament in 1643 at a time of profound political and ecclesiastical upheaval. The assembly was tasked with recommending reforms to the doctrine, worship, government, and discipline of the Church of England. After more than five years of careful biblical study and theological deliberation, the assembly produced the Westminster Confession of Faith along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Together, these documents have served as the doctrinal foundation of Presbyterian churches throughout the world for nearly four centuries. The assembly’s influence, however, extends far beyond Presbyterianism. The confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. As a result, its theological influence shaped generations of Congregationalists, Baptists, and other evangelical Christians. The editors of this volume rightly observe, The confession is also ecumenical because it found wide acceptance among Congregationalists and Particular Baptists in the seventeenth century, as two different groups of theologians adapted the confession according to their theological convictions, producing the Savoy Declaration (1658) and the Second London Confession (1689). Thus the Westminster Confession is relevant to Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists. (xx) Why Another Commentary? The Westminster Confession has never lacked commentators. From the 17th century onward, pastors and theologians have written to explain its theology. Quality works by A. A. Hodge , G. I. Williamson, R. C. Sproul, and more recently Chad Van Dixhoorn have each served the church well in different ways. So why do we need another commentary on the confession, and what makes this one useful? The Westminster Confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. First, this isn’t the work of a single author but a collaborative effort by scholars whose expertise spans several areas of theology. That breadth allows the volume to approach the confession from different perspectives while maintaining a clear unity of purpose. Each contributor brings particular expertise to the section he addresses, but the volume as a whole is concerned with helping readers understand the confession and its significance for the church. Second, the commentary is consciously pastoral. Rather than treating the confession merely as a historical artifact or an academic text, the contributors consistently demonstrate how its theology serves the life of the church. Readers are reminded that the confession was written not simply to settle theological disputes but to help the church understand and live out the whole counsel of God. This pastoral emphasis matters. It’s easy for a confession to become something we study without allowing it to shape the way we live as Christians. The Westminster Confession was never intended to be a document we merely admire or defend. Its doctrines are meant to shape the faith of the church as we “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 1:3). This commentary is useful because it helps readers make that connection, showing not only what the assembly confessed but why those truths matter today. Faith with Roots As a pastor, I’m finding that one of the great needs of our day is a sense of rootedness. Many Christians are looking for something that will give them a deeper sense of stability and connection to the historic Christian faith, something that didn’t begin with the latest movement or cultural moment. They’re looking for something with roots. It’s easy for a confession to become something we study without allowing it to shape the way we live as Christians. This is one of the gifts of the Westminster Confession of Faith. Its doctrinal roots have given generations of believers a lasting stability, keeping them grounded in the historic faith through waves of theological and cultural change. It doesn’t simply teach us what to believe; it roots those beliefs within the life of the church, connecting us to generations of faithful Christians who have confessed these same truths before us. The Westminster Confession helps us to see that we don’t have to find our footing in the Christian faith on our own. We receive the gift of learning from generations of believers who have gone before us, helping us see the riches of Scripture with greater clarity and confidence. This volume is an invitation to rediscover that heritage and to find fresh encouragement in the faithfulness of God, who has sustained his church through the centuries. May it help a new generation find joy in the riches of the Reformed tradition and pass them on with confidence to those who follow.

改革意味着什么? 标签经常使用,但并不总是谨慎。 对某些人来说,它只是提到救赎的特定观点. 对其他人来说,它引起一种传统、一种文化,甚至一种美学。 然而,从历史上看,改革意味着更加富有的东西。
虽然没有一句话能捕捉到被改造后的传统的全部,但至少它意味着三件事:是圣经,是盟约,是忏悔. 圣经的权威支配着我们的神学,盟约神学提供了圣经的红发框架,历史的忏悔总结并捍卫了教会的教义信念。
移除其中任何一根支柱,失去对改革后的传统至关重要的东西。 改革神学院长期试图在所有三个领域为牧师和教会成员提供教具, 近年来,该校院士编写了大量关于"旧约"和"新约"和"盟约神学"等著作.
现在,随着《威斯敏斯特信仰的忏悔:对其历史、神学和适用的综合评论》,他们把注意力转向改革后传统的忏悔基础。 结果的一卷不仅试图解释忏悔的教义,还试图表明为什么忏悔神学在今天仍然对教会至关重要.
韦斯敏斯特对信仰的忏悔是什么? 威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔会取而代之的是威斯敏斯特大会(Westminster Assembly),这是1643年英国议会在政治与教会剧变深刻的时期召开的由100多位部长和神学家组成的集会.
大会的任务是建议对英格兰教会的学说,崇拜,政府和纪律进行改革. 经过五年多的认真的圣经研究和神学审议后,大会产生了"威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔"(Westminster Confession of Faith)和"更大规模和更短的卡特克主义".
近四个世纪以来,这些文件共同成为全世界长老会教会的理论基础。 然而,议会的影响远远超出长老会。 忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革后传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架。
因此,它的神学影响塑造了几代基督教会,浸信会等福音派基督徒.
这本书的编辑们正确地指出,《忏悔书》也具有普世性,因为它在17世纪被基督教会和特定浸信会广泛接受,因为两个不同的神学家群体根据他们的神学信念修改了供词,产生了"萨伏依宣言"(1658年)和"第二次伦敦忏悔书"(1689年).
因此,威斯敏斯特忏悔与长老会、基督教会和浸信会有关。 (二十) 为什么另作一评注? 威斯敏斯特的"忏悔"从未缺少评论家. 从17世纪起,牧师和神学家都撰文解释其神学. 质量作品由A. A. Hodge, G. I. Williamson, R. C.
以及最近查德·范迪克斯霍恩以不同方式为教会服务。 因此,我们为什么需要关于供词的另一条评论,是什么使得这一条有用呢? 威斯敏斯特忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革后传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架.
首先,这不是一位作者的工作,而是学者的合作努力,他们的专业知识跨越了神学的几个领域。 这种宽度允许量从不同的角度对待供词,同时保持明确的目的一致。
每个贡献者都会为他所讲的一节带来特殊的专门知识,但该卷整体关注的是帮助读者理解忏悔及其对教会的意义. 第二,评注是自觉的放肆。
撰稿人不但没有将忏悔仅仅视为历史文物或学术文本,反而一贯表明其神学如何为教会的生活服务. 读者们被提醒,供词的写作不仅是为了解决神学上的争议,而且是为了帮助教会理解并活出整个上帝的劝告. 这种对牧业的重视很重要。
忏悔很容易成为我们研究的东西, 威斯敏斯特的忏悔书 从来都不是我们只崇拜或捍卫的文件 它的教义意在塑造教会的信仰,因为我们“延续着永远交给圣徒的信仰”(Jude 1:3)。
这篇评论很有用,因为它有助于读者建立这种联系,不仅表明大会承认了什么,而且表明这些真理为何今天重要。 对根的信念 作为牧师,我发现我们这个时代的伟大需求之一是一种扎根感。
许多基督徒正在寻找一些能让他们更深刻地感受到基督教历史信仰的稳定与联系的东西, 他们正在寻找有根的东西。 忏悔很容易成为我们研究的东西,
这是威斯敏斯特忏悔信仰的礼物之一. 它的理论根源使几代信徒获得持久稳定,通过神学和文化变革的浪潮,使他们建立在历史信仰的基础之上。 它并不只是教我们相信什么;
它将这些信仰植根于教会的生活中,将我们与几代忠实的基督徒联系起来,他们向我们坦白了同样的真理。 西敏的忏悔有助于我们发现我们不必靠自己找到基督教信仰的基础。
我们接受从我们之前的几代信徒那里学习的礼物,帮助我们更清楚地、更自信地看到天经的丰富之处。 这一卷是邀请人们重新发现这一遗产,并找到对上帝忠诚的新鼓励,上帝在几个世纪中一直维持着他的教堂.
愿它能帮助新一代人在改革后的传统财富中找到欢乐,并充满信心地将这些财富传给追随者。

featured.title: If the Church Did Its Job, Would the Parachurch Exist?
featured.summary: Do pregnancy centers, food pantries, or campus ministries exist because the church is failing to do her work?
featured.summary_zh: 我听到它不止一次地说 : “ 如果教会完成了它的工作, 例如,我在咨询一位当地牧师,他希望看到教堂为他所在社区的穷人服务。 对他来说重要的是,教会必须这样做,而不是非营利组织。 由于他知道上帝的王国比他的会众还大,他想让多个教会参与这个项目. 我建议他考虑成立一个牧师理事会,并集体雇用一名工作人员来管理合并方案的运作。
featured.title_zh: 如果教会做了它的工作，教堂会存在吗？
featured.content: I’ve heard it said more than once: “If the church did its job, the parachurch wouldn’t have to exist.” For instance, I was consulting with a local pastor who wanted to see the church serve people in poverty in his community. It was important to him that the church do it, not a nonprofit. Since he understood that God’s kingdom is bigger than his congregation, he wanted to engage multiple churches in the project. I suggested he consider forming a council of pastors and collectively hiring a staff member to manage the operations of the combined program. He thought that could work well for his context. I’m not sure he was aware of the irony. I certainly was: We’d just reinvented a variant of the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that he so keenly wanted to avoid in the first place. While the allergy to faith-based nonprofits was especially strong in his case, many people accept the premise at a basic level. In my experience, this sentiment is just as likely to come from someone who works in nonchurch ministry as from a pastor. If we understand the church is the core institution created by Christ to advance the kingdom of heaven, has it failed so badly that we need an army of auxiliaries to prop it up? Clarifying Terms and Roles I answer that the parachurch doesn’t exist because the church has failed. It exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. Proving that starts with clarifying terms. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. “Church” has more than one use in Scripture. In some contexts, it describes the people of God universally (Matt. 16:15–18; Eph. 1:22–23; Col. 1:18). In others, it’s a local congregational institution with the parameters God has placed around its operation (1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “Parachurch” typically refers to faith-based nonprofits who serve people in need or provide evangelistic and discipleship resources. Certainly, as part of the universal church, all God’s people hold equal status in advancing God’s mission, whether they labor as nurses, students, pastors, or tentmakers (see Acts 18:1–3). Just as surely, all God’s people shouldn’t merely attend but be accountable to a local congregation that enables their spiritual formation. When not assembled, God’s people are charged with many tasks—everything from stewarding creation to seeking justice for the oppressed. We can fulfill these tasks as individuals, but it often makes sense to create or join institutions dedicated to fulfilling them. Which brings us to a crucial point: God ordained some institutions specifically, and some emerged organically from God’s commands. Ordained or Emergent Institutions The family, the local church, and the government are ordained institutions. The Bible gives each ordained institution some guidance but also leaves a lot open to interpretation. While these ordained institutions are necessary for all people, they aren’t sufficient to fulfill God’s myriad commands to their fullest extent. Thus, some institutions emerge from the commands, rather than from a revealed institutional structure: The command to work led to the formation of businesses. The command to pass knowledge to subsequent generations led to the formation of schools. The command to care for the sick caused Christians to form the first hospitals. The command to care for the poor, widows, orphans, and strangers led to the formation of charities . The command to make disciples of all nations led to mission boards, publishing houses, and Bible-translation ministries. This ordained-emergent distinction parallels Abraham Kuyper’s “ sphere sovereignty ” in its recognition of institutions not explicitly outlined in Scripture. Many of these commands can be fulfilled to some lesser degree by the ordained institutions, but there are limitations. A family may work without forming a business, but they’ll never raise a skyscraper. Most believers recognize that the bulk of emergent institutions are legitimate. No one says, “If the church did its job being hospitable, restaurants wouldn’t need to exist.” Similarly, I don’t hear a lot of people saying, “If the church cared for the sick, hospitals wouldn’t need to exist.” Businesses, schools, hospitals, and charities all work best when operated by believers in accordance with God’s precepts. But they don’t have to answer to a plurality of elders any more than they have to be structured like a family whose children must answer to their parents. Churches, Nonprofits, and Businesses Ordained institutions have distinct mandates that limit what other institutions should do. That’s why Paul instructs Timothy that the local church shouldn’t aid a widow who has a family capable of aiding her (1 Tim. 5:3–4). Without question, overeager nonprofits at times impinge on the core duties of a family or local church. But in general, emergent institutions are legitimate and complement the work of the government, congregation, and family. Ordained institutions have distinct mandates that limit what other institutions should do. The Bible acknowledges this by its support of businesses . While the command to work is ordained by God, Scripture nowhere defines a prescriptive business structure. Yet the employer-employee relationship is acknowledged as legitimate, and the institution as one that promotes human flourishing. Once for-profit entities aren’t viewed as a local congregation’s failure, the line between a kingdom-minded business and a kingdom-minded nonprofit becomes fuzzy. For instance, plenty of for- and nonprofit enterprises intentionally employ and disciple people who are difficult to employ. Surely the tax structure doesn’t determine the theological validity of the enterprise. Thus, claims like “God created the church; he didn’t create the pregnancy resource center”—while true in the most literal sense—don’t communicate much of value. It’s a bit like saying, “God made trees. He didn’t make your table.” My table is made almost entirely of trees. The table is a good thing for which I should be grateful to God. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. The more the church does its job, the more local congregations there will be, the more nonprofits there will be, and the more redemptive businesses there will be. The question isn’t whether the church should replace the parachurch but whether God’s people will faithfully build every institution needed to accomplish his will.
featured.content_zh:
我听到它不止一次地说 : “ 如果教会完成了它的工作, 例如,我在咨询一位当地牧师,他希望看到教堂为他所在社区的穷人服务。 对他来说重要的是,教会必须这样做,而不是非营利组织。
由于他知道上帝的王国比他的会众还大,他想让多个教会参与这个项目. 我建议他考虑成立一个牧师理事会,并集体雇用一名工作人员来管理合并方案的运作。 他认为这对他的背景来说是可行的。 我不确定他是否意识到讽刺。
我当然是:我们刚刚重新发明了501(c)(3)非营利的变体,他一开始非常想避免它。 虽然在他的案件中对基于信仰的非营利组织特别过敏,但许多人在基本层面上接受了这一前提。 根据我的经验,这种情绪可能来自在非教会部工作的人和牧师。
如果我们理解教会是基督为推进"天国"而建立的核心机构,那么它是否如此地失败了,以至于我们需要一支辅军来支撑它? 我回答说教区并不存在, 它的存在是因为上帝的命令自然产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。
证明从澄清条款开始。 教区之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 “教会”在《圣经》中有不止一种用途。 在某些情况下,它普遍描述了上帝的人民(Matt. 16:15–18;Eph. 1:22–23;Col. 1:18)。
在其他情况下,它是一个具有上帝设定参数的地方教会机构,围绕它的运作(1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3: 1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “教会”一般是指为有需要的人服务或提供福音和门徒资源的基于信仰的非营利组织。
当然,作为普世教会的一部分,所有上帝的人民在推进上帝的使命方面都具有同等的地位,无论是作为护士、学生、牧师还是帐篷匠(见第18:1至3号法案)。 诚然,所有上帝的信徒不应该只参加,而应该对能够形成精神的当地教会负责。
在没有集合的时候,真主的宗族将担负许多任务,从管理创造到为被压迫者寻求正义。 我们可以作为个人完成这些任务,但建立或加入专门履行这些任务的机构往往是合理的。 这让我们到了一个关键点:真主专门规定一些制度,有些制度是从真主的命令中有机地出现的。
组织或应急机构 家庭、地方教会和政府是法定机构。 《圣经》为每个指定机构提供了一些指导,但也为解释留下了很大余地。 尽管这些指定机构对所有人来说都是必要的,但它们不足以最充分地执行上帝的众多命令。
因此,有些机构产生于指挥部,而不是一个公开的体制结构: 工作指挥导致了企业的形成. 将知识传给后人的命令导致了学校的形成. 照顾病人的命令使得基督徒组成了第一批医院.
照顾穷人、寡妇、孤儿和陌生人的命令导致了慈善机构的成立。 使各国门徒的指挥导致了传教板,出版社,和圣经翻译部. 这一规定性的区别与亚伯拉罕·库伊珀的 " 领域主权 " 相似,因为它承认了《圣经》中没有明确阐述的机构。
许多这些命令在较低程度上可以由指定机构执行,但有一些限制。 一家人可以工作而不创业, 大多数信徒承认,大多数新兴机构是合法的。
没有人会说,“如果教会做好了自己的工作, “如果教会照顾病人, 医院就不需要存在。 企业、学校、医院和慈善机构在由信徒按照上帝的戒律运作时都做得最好。
也不必像家庭一样, 子女必须向父母负责。 教会、非营利和经商机构有不同的授权,限制其他机构应做什么。
这就是为什么保罗指示蒂莫西,当地教会不应该帮助一个有家庭能力帮助她的寡妇(1 Tim. 5:3–4). 毫无疑问,过度的非营利组织有时会损害家庭或地方教会的核心职责。 但总的来说,新兴机构是合法的,是对政府,会众和家庭工作的补充.
法定机构有不同的授权,限制其他机构应做什么。 《圣经》通过支持企业来承认这一点。 虽然工作命令由上帝下达,但《圣经》却无一规定一种规范的商业结构。 然而,雇主与雇员的关系被公认为合法,而这种关系是促进人类繁荣的机构。
一旦盈利实体不被视为当地众会的失败,一个有王国意识的企业和有王国意识的非营利之间的界线就会变得模糊不清。 例如,许多营利和非营利企业有意雇用难以雇用的人和门徒。 当然,税收结构并不决定企业的神学有效性。
因此,“上帝创建了教会;他没有创建孕期资源中心”之类的说法,尽管从最直白的意义上讲是真实的,但并没有传达多少价值。 这有点像“上帝造出树木。 他没有给你做桌子。 我的桌子几乎是树做的 桌子是件好事 我该感谢上帝
教区之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 教会的工作越多,当地的会会越多,非盈利性会越多,而红发会的企业也就越多.
问题不在于教会是否应该取代教区,

featured.summary_zh: Melissa和Courtney讨论如何在寻求建议时培养辨识力. 他们谈论我们有时认为我们需要信息, 当我们真正需要的是关系。 他们讨论他们喜欢从网络或ChatGPT获得什么样的建议, 为何不推荐给婚姻及养育等智慧问题, 资源参考:在您当地教会的相关资源中提供厨房-餐桌咨询:让我们谈谈:寻找导师和成为导师想要在智慧中成长?
featured.title_zh: 从互联网上获取建议的危险
featured.content: Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice. They talk about how sometimes we think we need information when what we really need is relationship. They discuss what kind of advice they like to get from the internet or ChatGPT, why they don’t recommend it for wisdom issues such as marriage and parenting, and why we shouldn’t let advice from AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ. Resource Mentioned: Kitchen-Table Counseling Within Your Local Church Related Resources: Let’s Talk: Finding a Mentor and Being a Mentor Want to Grow in Wisdom? You Need Gospel Friends. Why AI Parenting Advice Falls Short Don’t Treat AI as Your Pastor Discussion Questions: 1. When you face a difficult decision or struggle, where do you typically turn for advice? 2. How do you discern whether online advice is helpful or unwise? 3. What makes advice offered within a personal relationship different from advice taken from an online blog or influencer or generated by AI? 4. How might repeated exposure to ideas about marriage, parenting, or relationships on social media influence our thinking without us being aware of it? 5. What do we lose when we turn to online sources for counsel instead of investing in relationships with people who know and love us? 6. Who in your life knows you well enough to speak honestly into your decisions and loves you enough to do so? How can you cultivate those kinds of relationships? 7. How would you like to grow in your ability to offer wise counsel to others?

featured.title_zh: 小心让精神疾病成为一种身份
featured.content: In the years since he was involuntarily committed to a mental health institution for bipolar disorder, Frederik deBoer has wrestled with both profound gratitude for a system that saved his life and also palpable frustration that his experience of healing has become so rare. All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered is the latest broadside from one of the internet’s most heterodox thinkers and writers. As an “old school” Marxist best known for writing The Cult of Smart , deBoer takes aim at how the cultural drift within his own tribe is responsible for making mental health care so elusive for those who need it most: “The tendency to treat mental illness as an exciting adventure, the endless romanticization of lunacy in popular culture, is one of many aggravations I have nursed for years” (8). The root of his aggravation—the treatment of mental illness and disability as an identity to be celebrated rather than a disability that needs treatment —isn’t all in his head. The use of talk therapy rose 47 percent between 2019 and 2024 . A 2025 LifeStance survey found around 29 percent of U.S. adults have self-diagnosed their mental health condition after consuming online content, rising to 50 percent among Gen Z (versus 9 percent of boomers). Of the people who self-diagnose symptoms, almost a quarter (24 percent) “rarely” or “never” feel the need to take the next step to discuss them with a qualified clinician. DeBoer argues that rather than reducing the stigma surrounding mental illness, the inordinate attention given to the mildly and dubiously afflicted is a dangerous distraction crowding out help for the severely ill. Accelerated by social media, this “gentrification of disability” has become a full-blown social contagion, compromising even the experts and institutions responsible for mental health care (153–54). DeBoer is largely right, and the cultural shift he identifies has real-world implications both inside and outside the church. But the same ideological priors that so sharpen deBoer’s critique also suffer from two significant blind spots that, were they addressed, would make All in Your Head the more courageous, more constructive, and, therefore, more widely read manifesto we need. General Bipartisan Ire If you picked up All in Your Head to understand how modern therapy culture spread like wildfire across social media over the last several years, it’s not immediately obvious why deBoer starts his argument with an in-depth analysis of the anti-psychiatry movement’s influence in late 20th century politics and academia. But, if you can forgive me the pun, there’s a method to his madness. After a blistering critique of “rightwing libertarian” policies that neglected mental illness, he cashes in on the subsequent trust he earns with left-leaning readers to launch a series of absolute haymakers toward “a species of thought that sometimes amounts to a kind of leftist pseudo-radicalism or a libertarian fantasy” (198) that drives the “destabilizing . . . move from mental illness as reality to mental illness as symbol” (8). American individualism and anti-institutional bias aren’t new, but the painstakingly specific way deBoer traces their spread through the culture surrounding mental health and therapy is refreshing and instructive. Our “apolitical romanticism of resistance to modern society” fuels two opposite errors: On the right, mental illness is sometimes seen as either imagined or a symptom of weak character. But on the left, the same romanticism often describes mental disability as more en abling than dis abling, as if neurodivergent minorities don’t need society’s help—society needs theirs. Gentrification of Disability DeBoer’s emphatic rejection of this predominantly progressive error— of “making a medical disorder an identity”—is the “overarching principle of [his] book” (165). This is never more clear in what he labels “the gentrification of disability,” where “diagnoses become fads” because the “intellectual and discursive space once dedicated to the interests of the most afflicted have become fixated instead on a class of patients whose disorders range from mild to dubious” (154). Said spaces and institutions have become so compromised due to “the diseased incentives of social media” and “liberal conventional wisdom that says it’s offensive to question any claim any individual makes about a disability.” Combined, “we’ve created ‘disorder communities’” not unlike fan clubs “rooting for a particular sports team” (154). The disproportionate attention given to those wealthy enough or high-functioning enough to perform their disability online is a dangerous distraction with real consequences: The more that influential elites use their status to “define the disorder in the public mind,” the more those who are impoverished or severely disabled go unseen and neglected. The disproportionate attention given to those wealthy enough or high-functioning enough to perform their disability online is a dangerous distraction with real consequences. Clear to anyone not living under a rock for the last decade is how familiar these patterns are. As I argued in The Reason for Church , counterfeit institutions (e.g., social media) have bypassed gatekeepers and hijacked the incentives of vital social and spiritual institutions undergirding American life. All in Your Head won’t add many new tools for recognizing these patterns. DeBoer’s contribution is in tracing them throughout an often convoluted bureaucratic ecosystem from the perspective of a “crabby old Marxist” frustrated by the privileged hypocrisy of pop-critical theory and progressive politics. However useful, the same ideological priors also handicap his analysis with two glaring omissions. Incomplete Diagnosis and Insufficient Prescription His most obvious omission is the rapid rise of gender dysphoria diagnoses and sex-reassignment surgery for minors. For more than a decade, gender-affirming physicians have been telling parents they must choose between having “a trans kid or a dead kid,” but, as Rebecca McLaughlin points out , the evidence says otherwise: “Puberty blockers can make the mental health of some young people worse, not better.” Considering deBoer’s impressive track record of taking unpopular, heterodox positions within his own tribe, his failure to address what is arguably the most volatile and life-altering consequence of toxic therapy culture is bewildering. DeBoer’s second omission is more understandable. While he concludes with well-reasoned (if regrettably materialist and socialist) policy prescriptions, he doesn’t offer any remedy for the broader therapeutic culture (i.e., the “ideological commitment to radical individual autonomy” [77]) that he spends most of the book arguing is the root of resistance to reform. That neglect robs his policy prescriptions of much persuasive power. Christians can affirm deBoer’s diagnosis of the problem of individual autonomy, but the church has the social and spiritual resources missing from all legislative and policy prescriptions. We know humans were never meant to construct our identities but to receive them in Christ and through belonging to our families, to our churches, and ultimately to God. Church has the social and spiritual resources missing from all legislative and policy prescriptions. Despite any omissions, All in Your Head is a clear-eyed and validating read, especially for those in (or disappointed by) mental health care. It would be a fine complement to Matthew Loftus’s Resisting Therapy Culture and describes many of the downstream problems Philip Rieff anticipated in The Triumph of the Therapeutic . All in Your Head is “not a memoir” (8) but a pragmatic antimemoir seething with a holy discontent that challenges both performative mental illness and the also voyeurism that incentivizes it. featured.content_zh:
在他非自愿地被送入精神病院治疗两极分化后的几年里,弗雷德里克·德·博尔带着对挽救他生命的系统深表感谢和明显的沮丧,因为他的治愈经验变得如此罕见.
在你的脑海中:作为身份的疾病,作为时尚的创伤,以及希望陷入混乱,是互联网上最异形的思想家和作家之一的最新一面。
作为一位最以写作"聪明的邪教"而出名的"老派"马克思主义者,德博尔以自己的部落内部的文化漂移为目的,让那些最需要的人如此难以接受精神保健:"将精神疾病视为激动人心的冒险的倾向,在流行文化中无休止地浪漫化的放荡,是多年来我所照顾的诸多恶化之一"(8).
他的病情恶化的根源——将精神疾病和残疾视为一种值得庆贺的身份,而不是需要治疗的残疾——并不是他脑子里所有的东西。 2019年至2024年间,谈话疗法的使用率上升了47%. 2025年生活稳定调查发现美国约有29%的人口.
成人在消费在线内容后自行诊断其心理健康状况,在Gen Z中上升到了50%(相对于9%的繁荣者)。 在自我诊断的人群中,近四分之一(24%)的人“勉强”或“从未”感到有必要采取下一步措施,与合格的临床医生讨论这些症状。
DeBoer认为,对受轻度和可疑折磨的人的过度关注,与其减少精神疾病的污名化,不如说是一种危险的分心,挤出对重病患者的帮助。
社交媒体加速了这种 " 残疾意识化 " ,已成为一种全面的社会传染,甚至损害负责精神保健的专家和机构(153-54)。 DeBoer基本上是正确的,他所认定的文化转变在教堂内外都具有现实世界的影响.
但德布尔批评如此尖锐的意识形态前科也遭遇了两个重大盲点,如果这些盲点得到解决,将使你的头脑更加勇敢,更具建设性,因此,我们需要更广泛地阅读宣言。
一般两党爱尔兰人 如果你在脑海中看到现代治疗文化在过去几年里如何像野火一样在社交媒体上传播,那么DeBoer为什么以深入分析20世纪后期反精神病运动在政治和学术界的影响为出发点,这并不明显。
但是,如果你能原谅我的双关语,他疯狂是有办法的。
在对忽略了精神疾病的“右翼自由派”政策猛烈批评后,他依靠后来对左翼读者的信任,发动了一系列绝对的干草者,走向“有时相当于左翼伪激进主义或自由派幻想的思想”(198年),推动“稳定......”。
从精神疾病作为现实转变为精神疾病作为象征”(8)。 美国的个人主义和反机构偏见并非新事物, 但DeBoer通过精神卫生与治疗的文化,
我们“反对现代社会的政治浪漫主义”助长了两个相反的错误: 在右边,精神疾病有时被视为一种想象或一种弱性症状. 但是在左边,同样的浪漫主义常常将精神残疾描述为比分身更困难,仿佛神经分身的少数民族不需要社会的帮助——社会需要他们的帮助。
对DeBoer残疾人的强烈反对,即 " 使医疗障碍成为身份 " 这一主要进步的错误,是 " 书中的首要原则 " (165)。
在他所谓的“残疾的基因化”中,这一点再清楚不过了,因为“曾经专为受感染最深的人的利益服务的智慧和模糊空间已经固定在一类疾病从轻度到可疑的病人身上”(154个)。
因为“社会媒体的有病刺激”和“自由传统智慧, 综合起来, " 我们创建了`混乱社区 ' " ,与粉丝俱乐部 " 为某一特定体育队 " (154个)不同。
对足够富有或高运作能力的人的过度关注, 有影响力的上层人士越是利用其地位“界定公众心中的混乱”,穷人或严重残疾者就越是被忽视和忽视。
对那些足够富有或高功用、足以在线处理残疾的人的过度关注是一种危险的分心,会产生实际后果。 过去十年里没有生活在岩石下的人很清楚 这些模式是多么熟悉。
假冒机构(如社交媒体)绕过守门人, 并劫持了影响美国生活的重要社会及精神机构。 在你的脑海中,
DeBoer的贡献在于从一个被流行批评理论和进步政治的特有伪善所挫败的“疯狂的老马克思主义者”的视角来追踪整个经常被曲解的官僚生态系统。 不管多么有用,同样的意识形态前科也以两个明显的遗漏来阻碍他的分析。
未完全诊断和处方不足 他最明显的遗漏是性别障碍诊断和未成年人性转移手术的迅速上升.
十多年来,具有性别特征的医生一直告诉父母,他们必须在“一个跨性别的孩子或一个已经死亡的孩子”之间做出选择,但是,正如Rebecca McLaughlin所指出,证据却说道 : “ 纯洁的阻塞者可以使一些年轻人的精神健康恶化,而不是更好。 ” 考虑到德博尔在自己的部落中 占据不受欢迎的异教徒地位 令人印象深刻的记录
他未能解决毒药治疗文化 带来的最不稳定、最改变生命的后果, DeBoer的第二次遗漏更让人理解。
虽然他最后给出了合理(如果令人遗憾的是唯物主义和社会主义)政策处方,但他并没有为更广泛的治疗文化(即“激进个人自主的意识形态承诺”[77])提供任何补救,他花在书中的大部分争论是抵制改革的根源。 这种忽视剥夺了他的政策处方 很大的说服力。
基督徒可以肯定DeBoer对个人自治问题的诊断,但教会在所有立法和政策处方中都缺少社会和精神资源。 我们知道人类从来就不是要建立我们的身份,而是要在基督中,通过属于我们的家庭、我们的教会以及最终属于上帝来接受他们。
教会在所有立法和政策规定中都缺少社会和精神资源。 尽管有任何疏漏,但《你的头脑》是一个清晰而真实的读物,特别是对于接受(或因)精神保健的人来说。
并描述了Philip Rieff在《治疗的凯旋》中预料到的许多下游问题。 你脑子里全是“不是回忆录”(8),而是一种务实的预言,充满了圣洁的不满,既挑战了表现性精神疾病,也挑战了刺激这种疾病的巫术。
结果是以令人印象深刻的解释对心理健康文化进行了具体和令人信服的再规划。
featured.author: Brad Edwards

featured.title: How a Former Prisoner in Iran Wants You to Pray for Christians in Chains
featured.summary: Pray not only for what God might do for Christian prisoners in Iran but for what God might do through them, for his glory.
featured.summary_zh: 不久前,我和两名基督教青年在伊朗最困难的监狱之一服刑。 因为他们拒绝停止宣扬耶稣。 我问自己如何为他们祈祷, 他们说,“祈祷我们在这里的工作结束前不会被释放。 ”
featured.title_zh: 伊朗前囚犯如何希望你为被锁的基督徒祈祷
featured.content: Not long ago, I had a surreal phone call with two young Christian men serving prison sentences in one of Iran’s hardest prisons. They’re there because they refuse to stop preaching about Jesus. When I asked how I could pray for them, their answer wasn’t what you might expect. “Pray that we would not be released until our job here is finished,” they said. They had led numerous fellow prisoners to faith. Now, their chief concern was to remain inside long enough to disciple them. The call took me straight back to the five years I spent in prison for my faith. Now, these dear brothers (let’s call them Vahid and Reza) were behind bars, and I was outside. As we spoke, I pictured the wards and corridors, imagined the sounds and smells, and remembered how hard it was not to know how many years I would be there. But it was also an encouraging call. Vahid and Reza were in high spirits, talking about Bible passages that were sustaining them and how the Lord was at work. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. Their focus was the same as Paul’s in Colossians 4:3: “Pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison.” Paul’s request wasn’t for an open prison door but for an open door for the gospel. Pray for Gospel Fruit Vahid and Reza’s request resonated with me. I remember being unable to pray for my own release. I tried on a few occasions, but I couldn’t open my mouth to ask the Lord to release me. If I’m following Christ, I cannot choose the path. I cannot choose the location. I should follow him wherever he goes. And as I followed him to prison, he brought beautiful fruit. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. I think of one prisoner, a devout Muslim, who was wrongly accused of spying for Iran’s enemies. He was praying he would be released and was frustrated to get no answer. He approached me one day, saying, “Farshid, our God is dead. But I’ve heard yours is alive. Will you pray for me?” Fearing it might be a trap, I took him quietly aside and prayed briefly in the name of Jesus: “Lord, you know this man. Please hear his prayer.” The very next day, the man rushed over excitedly and gave me a huge hug. That morning, he had learned his name had been cleared. He was released two weeks later. Our God is indeed alive. The Lord was also at work softening my parents’ hearts toward Christ during those years. I always say that even if only for the salvation of my parents, my time in prison was worth it. So, when you pray for persecuted believers, pray not only for what God might do for them but—as Vahid and Reza requested—for what God might do through them, for his glory. Pray for gospel fruit. Pray for Comfort and Endurance I don’t want to make prison sound easier than it was. The suffering was real. So pray also for comfort and endurance. They beat me; they broke my toe. But the prolonged separation from my two children was the hardest burden to bear. The day I went to prison, my son was 2 years old and my daughter was 7. Missing their childhoods was an unspeakable loss. Yet I know others who have suffered much more than I did. I think of a brother currently in prison who has been tortured. I think of a sister who was sexually assaulted when she was arrested. Even the apostle Paul was at times “so utterly burdened beyond [his] strength that [he] despaired of life itself.” And his request to the church was simple: “You also must help us by prayer” (2 Cor. 1:8, 11). Brothers and sisters like these need us to pray for them with love. Whatever the situation, we can pray that God would grant the suffering believer comfort, peace, and endurance. The more specific the prayers, the better. While in prison, I received letters from people around the world who were praying for me. One wrote, “I am praying for your sleep. May the Lord give you peace to sleep well in prison.” I really loved it. And honestly, I did sleep well in prison; many inmates suffered from nightmares, but I cannot remember having a single one. I believe God answered that man’s prayers. Your Prayers Reach Through Prison Walls Prayer is especially needed when a prisoner is in solitary confinement. I spent 361 days in a solitary cell: For a year, I couldn’t see the sun in the sky. Yet prayers reached me through the prison walls. I remember one day I was in cell 73. I was sitting; I wasn’t praying. Suddenly, I was able to hear, let me say, a heavenly melody in my soul—not in my ears but in my soul. And I stood up. In that moment, I was overwhelmed by joy and peace. I started dancing. The cell was only two meters by two meters, but I danced before the Lord! The guard opened the door to see what I was doing. I turned to him with a wide smile and said, “Hey, sir, how are you today?” He looked at me with big eyes. “Wow, it seems you are better than me,” he said. And then he shut the door. For a year, I couldn’t see the sun in the sky. Yet prayers reached me through the prison walls. I believe someone, or maybe a group of people, was praying for me at that time. That’s why I had the experience of hearing that melody in my soul, and I was overwhelmed by joy, even though I was in solitary confinement. Many brothers and sisters around the world prayed for me during my imprisonment. Perhaps you were one of them. I cannot find the words to say thank you. Now, I want to ask, Will you pray for those in prison right now for their faith? Scripture tells us to “remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them” (Heb. 13:3). I believe your prayer goes through the prison walls. It can touch the prisoners, encourage them, and give them joy while they’re suffering, because it’s possible to have joy and suffering at the same time. Vahid and Reza are just two of the Christians in Iran’s prisons today. There are so many. Maybe you’re asking, Where do I start? Elam’s free Bound Together resources can help your church or small group pray on the International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church on November 1. We pray because our God is faithful to his children. He is faithful right now to Vahid and Reza and to all our brothers and sisters in prison. And he was faithful to me. When I came out of prison, people would say to me, “Praise God, Farshid, you were faithful to the Lord. You stood for the Lord.” I always try to correct them. That’s not true. He was faithful to me. He stood for me.
featured.content_zh:
不久前,我和两名基督教青年在伊朗最困难的监狱之一服刑。 因为他们拒绝停止宣扬耶稣。 我问自己如何为他们祈祷, 他们说,“祈祷我们在这里的工作结束前不会被释放。”
他们带领许多同狱囚犯信仰。 现在,他们最关心的是 留在里面的时间足够长 让他们入门。 那通电话把我带回我为信仰在监狱里度过的五年。 现在,这些亲爱的兄弟(让我们叫他们Vahid和Reza)在监狱里,我在外面。
就在我们发言的时候,我想象了病房和走廊,想象了声音和气味,并想起了不知道我会在那里呆了多少年是多么困难。 但这也是一个令人鼓舞的呼吁。 瓦希德和礼萨精神高尚,谈论着支撑着他们的圣经段落,以及上帝是如何工作的. 他们并没有看到自己在一个悲惨而黑暗的地方。
他们看到自己在另一个任务领域。 他们的重心与保罗在Colosisans 4:3中的重心相同 : “ 也为我们祈祷,以便上帝为我们打开一个话语之门,宣告基督之谜,我为此而入狱。 ” 保罗的要求并不是打开监狱的门, 祈求福音果实Vahid,
我还记得我无法为自己的自由祈祷 我尝试过几次, 我无法选择道路。 我无法选择位置 我该跟着他 不管他去哪 当我跟着他进监狱时 他带来了美丽的水果 他们并没有看到自己在一个悲惨而黑暗的地方。
他们看到自己在另一个任务领域。 我想到一个囚犯, 一个虔诚的穆斯林, 他祈祷自己会被释放,并因得不到答复而感到沮丧。 有一天,他靠近我说,“法尔希德,我们的神死了。 但我听说你还活着。
你会为我祈祷吗?” 我担心那可能是一个陷阱,悄悄地把他放在一旁,以耶稣的名义简短地祈祷道:"主啊,你认识这个人。 请听他的祈祷。” 第二天,那个男人激动地冲过来,给了我一个巨大的拥抱。 那天早晨,他得知自己的名字已被清除。 他两周后被释放。 我们的神确实还活着。
在那些年中,上帝也在努力使我父母对基督的心软化。 我总是说,即使只是为了拯救我的父母, 我在监狱的时间是值得的。 当你们祈祷受迫害的信士们的时候,你们应当祈祷真主所意欲者,犹如瓦希德和里萨所意欲者那样,祈祷真主所意欲者。 祈取福音果实.

featured.title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
featured.content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. He says, “In any royal palace, you’re sure to find soldiers keeping watch over who and what has access to the very important king or queen inside”; those guards, he contends, are our habits, and “the strength of the soldiers determines how protected the palace is” (158). Early in the book, James calls teens to learn discernment. As he unpacks this habit, he warns them away from the siren song of social media influencers who question parental authority: “When an online influencer who doesn’t know you or care for you speaks about your parents or mentors in a way that makes you want to trust those people less and the influencer more, that’s a massive sign that what you’re listening to is false” (44). Yet James doesn’t merely tell young people to flee digital technology’s dangers; he also beckons them to put on habits that will help them cultivate virtue, in-person friendship, accountability, industrious work, creativity, and rest. For Parents Too Many of these habits are relational. In his introduction, for example, James encourages teens to read his book with a parent, teacher, pastor, or mentor. The discussion questions he includes at the end of each chapter make this counsel practical. This counsel is also wise, because while Scroll Less, Live More is a book for teens, it’s a book for parents too. As a parent and youth worker, I found James’s encouragement to develop a habit of self-awareness convicting. He calls readers to pay attention when being online leads to feelings of anger, anxiety, or boredom so that you know when to “log off and touch grass.” Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia : “Spiritual laziness that causes you to fill up on meaningless things so much that you cannot delight in God” (65). He nailed me. How many times do I fill life’s quiet moments—waiting in a line, a few minutes between meetings, or sadly even lulls in conversation—by pulling out my phone instead of being attentive to nature, the people around me, and the Lord? Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia . I can get frustrated when I see this tendency in teens, but as Brett McCracken writes , “What parents model with our own devices ultimately matters more than what we say to our kids about them.” James’s book helped me see ways I’ve failed to fight endless scrolling in my own life. As parents, we need God’s Spirit to help us grow in self-awareness about our tech habits. We need his grace to help us confess those failures to the teens we parent and lead. And we need a heart of wisdom and phone-stack intentionality, not just at youth group meetings but throughout our lives. Scroll Less, Live More helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.

featured.title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
featured.content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it. As a Christian and tech-policy analyst based in Washington, DC, where many of these conversations are taking place, I want to explain what effective altruism is, examine what it promises and where it fails to deliver, and show why this budding movement is incongruent with and a poor substitute for the gospel. What Is Effective Altruism? Effective altruism emerged in the late 2000s and early 2010s from the convergence of several intellectual movements, particularly utilitarian philosophy and evidence-based philanthropy. Australian academic Peter Singer provided an important foundation with his 1972 essay “ Famine, Affluence and Morality ,” where he argues that people have a moral obligation to prevent suffering when they can do so at relatively little cost to themselves. At its core, effective altruism is consequentialist, judging the rightness of an action chiefly by its outcomes. The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The Centre for Effective Altruism explains , “We’re committed to prioritizing actions that benefit more lives over actions that benefit a few—that saving a billion lives is more important than saving ten.” The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The movement took shape with the founding of several philanthropic organizations, such as GiveWell and 80,000 Hours . These groups emphasize measuring charitable impact, directing money toward the most effective actions, and choosing “high-impact” careers based on their potential to do good. Their approach to charitable giving has produced endeavors to improve global health , animal welfare , and economic disparities , among other areas. Over the past decade, effective altruism has expanded its scope, focusing on posterity and “longtermism,” the belief that “positively influencing the longterm future is a key moral priority of our time.” The Economist notes a belief this leads to: “Those not born yet should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are ‘longtermists’ who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.” This belief manifests itself in a focus on concerns such as existential risk (e.g., climate change or the next pandemic), nuclear proliferation, and artificial intelligence. For many in Silicon Valley, advanced AI is the defining problem of our day. The concern about a potential AI apocalypse explains why the movement has invested heavily in AI research, AI companies, and AI advocacy and safety. It’s not difficult to see why this philosophy has a natural audience among AI researchers and Silicon Valley tech luminaries. Effective altruism enables technologists to approach ethics in a way that can feel familiar: a series of probabilities, tradeoffs, and expected results—measuring an individual’s moral standing as mathematic calculations, similar to the process of building a software program where different inputs result in varied outputs. For ambitious individuals accustomed to solving complicated projects through ingenuity and critical analysis, this movement delivers reassuring community in an industry that often feels isolating. Adherents have a sense of higher purpose and calling as they’re suddenly confronted with extraordinary individual wealth and wrestle with the consequences of their technological discoveries. It’s hard to describe effective altruism without addressing its more eccentric views, some of which divide the movement itself. For example, the focus on animal welfare has led many in the movement to believe that any and all sentient beings share the same moral value, including but not limited to shrimp . Yes, since a dollar can go a long way to protect the well-being of a single crustacean , this cause could be the most efficient use of charitable giving. Notably, the effective altruist community has also drawn scrutiny for its sexual culture. A 2023 Time investigation highlighted how the movement’s overwhelmingly male membership, heavy overlap between work and home life, and its subculture of polyamory (which some have promoted as more rational than monogamy) has created a “culture of sexual harassment and abuse.” These dynamics have caused many—including Christians—to be concerned about the group’s outsize influence on culture. What Effective Altruism Promises (and Fails to Deliver) Effective altruism’s turn toward longtermism promises that the right people, armed with the right understanding of the stakes, can steer humanity safely through an uncertain future. Many in this community believe their adherence to consequentialism and longtermism gives them a special moral qualification to shape public policy. In their own eyes, effective altruists are the men and women of the hour. This conviction has moved from theory into practice. Political engagement by adherents has increased both on the public stage and backstage through building and funding civil society institutions to influence policymakers to embrace their ideology. One of the movement’s most prominent figures (though he has denied belonging to it), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, has been leaning on this philosophy to guide his leadership of his company and shape his approach to the future of AI . Yet for all its ambition, the movement struggles to deliver on what it promises. Effective altruism’s confidence in its own reasoning to navigate the future is a hubristic claim to possess unprecedented human knowledge. Any ethic that judges right and wrong by outcomes assumes we can reliably know what our actions will produce. It treats the future as a closed system of causes and effects that the right person or algorithm can calculate. But human knowledge is finite. We can’t trace the full effects of a single choice, much less forecast the welfare of billions of potential lives. At best, an outcome-based ethic can render its moral verdict only in hindsight. Most fundamentally, effective altruism fails us because it’s an ethic without a moral foundation. It has a laudable premise: Too many people around the globe are suffering, and those with means should help. Adherents can accurately quantify certain societal woes and calculate which actions could most efficiently produce the greatest benefit. But the philosophy largely assumes the moral obligations on which those calculations depend. In Singer’s foundational essay, he uses an illustration of a man wearing expensive sneakers who walks past a drowning child. He does a moral calculation that it’s better to save the child even if it ruins his shoes. The illustration works only because we already know the child matters and that walking past would be monstrous. But a strictly consequentialist framework can’t tell us why . If people are ultimately containers of welfare to be added up, then no one has worth in himself. Each matters only as a quantity in a calculation. And who decides which quantities count? Without an external source of moral truth, the answer is ultimately the individual. Each effective altruist must reason his way to his own conclusion about what “the most good” is, and no authority outside himself can tell him he’s wrong. Taken to its logical end, this leaves room for almost anything

在过去十年中,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷生根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是它的思想决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。
经济学人最近称这个哲学是“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称这个运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。 即使这种哲学正在推动市场和形成全球辩论,许多基督徒对它并不熟悉。
作为总部设在华盛顿特区的基督教和技术政策分析者,我想解释一下这些对话是何等有效的利他主义,审视它所承诺的以及它未能兑现之处,并表明为什么这个萌芽的运动与福音不相干,并且是一个糟糕的代名词。 什么是有效的替代主义?
2000年代后期和2010年代初,有效的利他主义从几个知识运动,特别是功利主义哲学和以证据为基础的慈善活动趋同而出.
澳大利亚学者彼得·辛格以他1972年的论文"饥荒,富裕和道德"为重要基础,他在该作中认为,当人们能够以相对较少的代价来预防痛苦时,他们有道德义务. 有效的利他主义的核心是结果主义,主要根据其结果判断行动是否正确。
有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。
“有效替代主义中心”解释说,“我们致力于优先考虑有利于更多生命的行动,而不是有利于少数人的行动——拯救十亿生命比拯救十亿生命更重要。 ” 有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。
随着几个慈善组织的成立, 这些团体强调衡量慈善影响,将资金用于最有效的行动,并根据他们做好事的潜力选择“高影响”职业。
他们的慈善捐赠方法 带来了改善全球卫生、动物福利和经济差距的努力。
在过去的十年中,有效的利他主义扩大了它的范围,把重点放在后人和“长期主义”上,认为“积极影响长期的未来是我们时代的主要道德优先事项”。 《经济学家》指出,这导致了一种信念:“那些尚未出生的,应该加以权衡,而且可能有上万亿美元。
许多职业介绍所是“长期主义者 ” , 他们认为他们有义务在遥远的将来预防风险, 即使这饿死今天的好原因, 这种信念表现在关注存在风险(如气候变化或下个大流行病)、核扩散和人工智能等关注。
对硅谷的许多人来说,先进的AI是我们当今的决定性问题. 对AI可能启示录的担忧解释了为什么该运动在AI研究、AI公司以及AI的倡导和安全方面投入了大量资金. 为何这个哲学在AI研究人员和硅谷科技流派中有自然的读者,
有效的利他主义使技术专家能够以能够感到熟悉的方式处理伦理问题:一系列概率、取舍和预期结果 -- -- 衡量个人的道德地位作为数学计算,类似于建立一个软件程序的过程,不同投入导致不同的产出。
对于习惯于通过智慧和批判性分析解决复杂项目的野心勃勃的个人来说,这一运动在一个常常感到孤立的行业中为社区带来安慰。 坚持者有更高的目的感, 并召唤他们突然面对着非凡的个人财富,
很难描述有效的利他主义, 例如,由于注重动物福利,运动中许多人认为,任何和所有神灵生物都具有同样的道德价值,包括但不限于虾类。
是的,因为一美元对保护单一甲壳类动物的福祉有很长的路要走,因此这一事业可能是慈善捐赠的最有效用途。 值得注意的是,有效的利他主义社区也对其性文化进行了审查。
2023年时间调查凸显了该运动绝大多数男性成员、工作与家庭生活严重重叠、以及其多元文化(有些人提倡这种文化比一夫一妻制更合理)如何创造了“性骚扰和性虐待文化 ” 。 这些动态导致包括基督教徒在内的许多人担心该团体对文化的影响过大。
有效的利他主义向长期主义的转变会保证,以正确理解利害关系为武装的正确人民能够安全地引导人类度过一个不确定的未来。 这个社区的许多人认为,他们坚持后果主义和长期主义,使他们具有制定公共政策的特殊道德资格。
在他们自己的眼中,有效的利他主义者是时空的男女. 这种信念已经从理论转变为实践。 通过建立和资助民间社会机构来影响决策者接受其意识形态,信徒在公共舞台和后台的政治参与都有所增加。
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei(虽然他否认属于这个运动)最有名的人物之一, 然而,运动的雄心壮志却在努力兑现它的承诺。
有效的利他主义相信它自己为未来航行的推理,是一种傲慢地宣称拥有前所未有的人类知识。 通过结果判断对错的任何伦理都假定我们能够可靠地知道我们的行动将产生什么。 它把未来视为一个封闭的由正确人或算法可以计算的因果关系系统. 但人类的知识是有限的。
我们无法追踪单一选择的全部效果,更无法预测数十亿潜在生命的福祉。 充其量,基于结果的伦理只有在事后才能作出道德判断。 最根本的,有效的利他主义使我们失望,因为它是一个没有道德基础的伦理。
它有一个值得称赞的前提:全球有太多的人在受苦受难,那些有财力的人应当提供帮助。 坚持者可以准确地量化某些社会灾难,并计算哪些行动能够最有效地产生最大效益。 但哲学基本上承担了这些计算所依赖的道德义务。
在Singer的基礎作文中,他用一幅插图,说明一个穿昂贵运动鞋的人走过一个被淹死的孩子. 他做了一个道德的计算, 认为救孩子更好, 这个插图之所以有效,只是因为我们已经知道儿童的重要性,而且走过去将是可怕的。 但严格地说,
如果人们最终是福利的容器 来加起来, 那么没有人有价值自己。 每种物质在计算中仅作为数量。 谁决定多少数量? 没有道德真理的外部来源,答案最终是个人.
每个有效的利他论者必须解释他自己对什么是“最美好的”的结论, 任何外部权威都不能告诉他自己错了。 顺理成章地说,这为几乎一切留下了空间

featured.content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. The playlist has 30 songs (one for each of November’s 30 days) expressing gratitude to God for our salvation in Christ, for the many blessings of marriage and family, and for the beauty of the earth. featured.title: The Voice of the Martyrs: Prayers of the Persecuted
featured.summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.
featured.summary_zh: " 耶和华说,多久? . . .
featured.title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
featured.content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. We pray the second petition of the Lord’s Prayer (“Thy kingdom come”) with the fifth petition also in mind (“Forgive us our debts”). Pray with a Desire for Repentance If God could turn his anger away from repentant sinners in exile (Ps. 79:5), then he could do the same for Israel’s enemies. While this is not explicit in Psalm 79, its near neighbor Psalm 83, at the conclusion of this section of Asaph psalms, prays that God would fill the faces of these enemy nations with shame “that they might seek [the LORD’s name]” (v. 16). It is legitimate to see this desire as qualifying the earlier imprecations in the Asaph collection (indeed, in the whole Psalter). Hamilton even suggests every prayer for judgment in the psalms should be read as if containing an implicit “footnote” desiring repentance as a possibility. Pray with the Hope of Final Justice The prayers of judgment, like Psalm 79, are not petty prayers incompatible with a Christian ethic. God’s people pray in response to horrific injustice, aimed at the glory of God, with a posture of humility and openness to their enemies becoming God’s friends. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. The imprecatory psalms, then, fit perfectly with the gospel of Jesus Christ. And they arm the church to intercede for the saints in a day when our Christian brothers and sisters suffer great harm throughout the world. We long for God to answer these prayers through the conversion of our enemies. But if they remain impenitent, it is only right for God to bring justice. And it is thus right for us to pray that he would.

他们以谦卑姿态祈祷正义,他们承认,除了上帝的恩惠外,这种判决也是他们应得的(vv.8-9)。 这与Luke 18:1–8中的遗孀祈求公道, 我们祈祷正义,但我们这样做是宽恕罪人。

虽然这在"诗经"79中并不明确,但它的近邻"诗经"83在"阿萨弗诗经"这一节的结尾,祈祷上帝会让这些敌国的脸充满羞耻"以"他们可能寻求[耶和华之名]"(v.16). 将这种愿望视为对阿萨夫集(事实上,整个Psalter)中早先的杂音加以限定是合理的.
汉密尔顿甚至建议,凡在诗文中为判断而祈祷的,都应理解为包含一个隐含的"脚注",希望作为可能的悔改. 与最终正义的希望祈祷 判断的祈祷与"诗经"79一样,并不是与基督教伦理格格不入的微小祈祷.
面对可怕的不公正,上帝的人民祈祷,以上帝的光荣为目标,以谦卑和对敌人的开放姿态成为上帝的朋友. 我们祈祷正义,但我们这样做是宽恕罪人。 浸信会的诗歌 完全符合耶稣基督的福音
他们武装教会,以便在我们基督教兄弟姐妹在世界各地遭受重大伤害的一天里,替圣徒们说情. 我们渴望上帝通过改变我们的敌人来回应这些祈祷. 但如果他们仍然无动于衷,那么上帝就应当伸张正义。 因此,我们祈祷他会这样做是正确的。
